stem: A pediatric pt with PUJO presentation with hydronephrosis, and asks about when to operate ?

opts.t: Decline in kidney function in MAG3

expl: UPJO is observed while the kidney drains and keeps its function; surgery (pyeloplasty) is indicated by a decline in split function on the MAG3 renal scan (< 40% or a fall > 10%), worsening dilatation, obstructed drainage or symptoms.

why.C: The degree of dilatation alone doesn't decide — dilated ≠ obstructed.
why.D: VUR is a different problem, managed on its own.

stem: Most common cause of antenatal hydronephrosis?
expl: UPJ obstruction is the commonest pathological cause of antenatal hydronephrosis (39–64% of unilateral ANH).

why.D: VUR is common (~a third) but second to UPJO.

stem: A 1-year-old girl presented with a history of documented recurrent febrile urinary tract infections. Renal and bladder ultrasounds were normal The micturating cystaurethrogram/MOUG)s shown in the picture, (pic of VUR) what is the initial treatment for this patient?
srcNote: (Antenatal hydronephrosis & common congenital genitourinary disorders) The source refers to an MCUG picture of VUR, but the image is not supplied in any of the matching source copies.
expl: Febrile UTIs with VUR in a 1-year-old → start continuous low-dose prophylactic antibiotics first; many cases resolve spontaneously, and prophylaxis is safe ("extended use is benign"). Surgery (Deflux or reimplantation) if breakthrough infections or high grade persisting.

why.A: Endoscopic (Deflux) comes after failure of prophylaxis or for high grade.
why.B: Observation alone after documented recurrent febrile UTIs risks renal scarring.
why.D: Open reimplantation is not the initial step.

stem: A newborn boy presented with history of bilateral antenatal hydronephrosis with thick bladder and dilated posterior urethra. What is the best radiologic study to diagnose the underlying pathology?
expl: Boy with bilateral hydronephrosis, thick bladder and dilated posterior urethra = posterior urethral valves → VCUG (MCUG) shows the dilated posterior urethra during voiding and any reflux.

why.C: US already showed the findings; it can't show the urethra while voiding.

stem: A 3 day neonate boy who was diagnosed with antenatal bilateral hydronephrosis on US , what is the next step in management?
srcNote: (Antenatal hydronephrosis & common congenital genitourinary disorders) Source note (Final 437 F Q56 (p. 91)): Newborn baby boy was diagnosed with bilateral hydronephrosis and mild oligohydramnios on antenatal US , what is the initial step in management ? A. Insert feeding tube A (Antenatal hydronephrosis & common congenital genitourinary disorders)
expl: Bilateral ANH in a newborn boy = PUV until proven otherwise → the first step is bladder drainage (urethral catheter), then NICU support, labs and antibiotics, and later valve ablation.

why.A: Antibiotics alone leave the obstruction undrained.
why.C: VCUG comes after the bladder is drained and the baby stabilized.
why.D: DMSA (function/scars) is not an early test.

stem: Newborn baby boy was diagnosed with bilateral hydronephrosis. US showed mild bladder wall hypertrophy, and a catheter was inserted. What is the best treatment option?
srcNote: (Antenatal hydronephrosis & common congenital genitourinary disorders) Only two choices are supplied in this source recall.
expl: After bladder drainage and stabilization, the definitive treatment of PUV is cystoscopic valve ablation.

opts.t: The child may have Poor stream

srcNote: , incomplete Q Incomplete source recall; no missing wording or options have been inferred.
expl: PUV obstructs the posterior urethra, so boys can present with a poor urinary stream and straining (besides antenatal diagnosis and UTIs).

why.A: Many are diagnosed antenatally, but not all — some present later.
why.C: Some present with UTI, but "diagnosed in childhood UTI" isn't the defining feature (and PUV is often found antenatally).
